title: Raga Tilang
hook: a raga with Persian color, where Guru Nanak speaks in words his Muslim neighbors used

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bairari, small enough to hear from start to finish, and your line was the whole of it. Did one thing get your whole attention? This week ends today: Jaitsri's quiet strength, Todi's tender morning, Bairari, and now Tilang. Day one thousand ninety-two.

Yak araj guftam pes tu. Those are the first words under the heading Raga Tilang, on ang seven twenty-one of the Guru Granth Sahib. Say them out loud and they don't sound like the Punjabi of the hymns before them. The words lean toward Persian, and a few lines later come names for God that Muslim neighbors in Guru Nanak's Punjab used. Same Guru, same book, same message. A different set of clothes. Today: Raga Tilang, and why a song might change its accent.
screen: `YAK ARAJ GUFTAM PES TU.` → `A DIFFERENT ACCENT.` → `SAME GURU, SAME BOOK.`

segments.voice: The ragas of the Granth come in a fixed order, and Tilang follows little Bairari. Its section opens with Guru Nanak. First, the plea itself, given here in plain English. I have made one petition before you; lend it your ear, Creator. Then the praise: you are true, great, generous, without flaw, the Sustainer. Then a hard turn. The world is a place you pass through; know it for certain, heart. The angel of death has me by the hair, and the heart hasn't understood. Second, the color. Listen to the names inside that praise: Karim, the generous one. Parvardigar, the one who sustains. Azrael, the angel of death. These are Persian and Arabic words, names for God and for the angel who comes at the end of life, that Muslims in Punjab used. Some readers hear Tilang as a place where Guru Nanak speaks to Muslim listeners in their own words. He doesn't argue with their vocabulary. He prays in it. The one God of the opening lines of the Granth is still the one being addressed. Only the accent has changed, the way a good host greets a guest in the guest's language. That's the persian color: not a different faith, a different set of words reaching for the same One. Third, the ending, which needs no translation into any accent. Nanak says: your servant is the dust under the feet of your servants. A petition that started by asking to be heard ends by asking to be low. In any language, the hymn's last move is humility.
screen: `TILANG FOLLOWS LITTLE BAIRARI.` · `ONE PLEA: LEND YOUR EAR, CREATOR.` · `KARIM, PARVARDIGAR: PERSIAN COLOR.` · `THE DUST UNDER YOUR SERVANTS' FEET.` · then, large: `PERSIAN COLOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Tilang, or to the words someone else uses for what matters. If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Tilang and let it run. If not, sit quietly. Bring to mind one person whose words for the deepest things are different from yours: a neighbor, a coworker, a grandparent. Don't translate them. Just hear them, the way they'd say it, and let those words be welcome for a while. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly. If you don't, simply let the other person's words rest beside your breath. The bell holds the time.
Raga Tilang. The raga after Bairari, where Guru Nanak's opening plea leans toward Persian and calls God Karim and Parvardigar. Today's word.

Your line: persian color. Today, when someone names something you care about in words that aren't yours, listen for what they're reaching for before you notice the words. Day one thousand ninety-two. A week done.
